# SecuPaste

> Post-quantum encrypted file sharing. Share files securely with ML-KEM (Kyber) + AES-256-GCM hybrid encryption.

SecuPaste is an open-source, privacy-first file sharing service that uses post-quantum cryptography to protect your files against both current and future threats, including quantum computers.

## Key Features

- **Post-Quantum Encryption**: Uses ML-KEM-768 (Kyber) + AES-256-GCM hybrid encryption
- **Client-Side Encryption**: All encryption/decryption happens in the browser — server never sees plaintext
- **Password Protection**: Argon2id key derivation with memory-hard protection against brute force
- **Decentralized Storage**: Files stored on Shelby Protocol for censorship resistance
- **Zero Knowledge**: Decryption keys are embedded in URL fragments (#) which are never sent to servers
- **File & Note Sharing**: Upload files or create encrypted text notes
- **Optional Metadata Encryption**: Encrypt filenames and file metadata

## Pages

- [Home](https://pastebin.sed.fyi/): Overview and feature highlights
- [Upload](https://pastebin.sed.fyi/upload): Upload and encrypt a file or create an encrypted note
- [Docs](https://pastebin.sed.fyi/docs): Technical documentation, security model, and FAQ

## Technical Specifications

- **Key Encapsulation**: ML-KEM-768 (Kyber) — NIST post-quantum standard
- **Symmetric Cipher**: AES-256-GCM with 96-bit nonce
- **Key Derivation**: Argon2id (64MB memory, 3 iterations, parallelism 1)
- **Salt Length**: 32 bytes, cryptographically random
- **Maximum File Size**: 100 MB
- **Link Validity**: 24 hours
- **Storage Backend**: Shelby Protocol (decentralized)

## Security Model

The security model is built on **zero knowledge** principles:

- File contents are always encrypted before upload
- Your password never leaves your device
- The decryption key lives in the URL fragment (after #), which per RFC 3986 is never sent in HTTP requests
- Even if servers are fully compromised, files remain secure
- Protected against: server breaches, man-in-the-middle attacks, future quantum computers, brute force attacks
